content: If the spray output increases by more than 10%, the nozzle must be replaced to prevent excessive discharge of the spray liquid, which could result in over-application of insecticide. Additionally, the operator should evaluate the spray distribution by spraying water onto a dry surface, moving the nozzle from the top to the bottom of a wall while maintaining a distance of 45–50 cm from the surface. The wetting pattern on the surface should indicate whether the spray is evenly distributed over a swath approximately 75 cm wide. The durability of the nozzles can be tested by spraying a suspension of silica powder in water, as described in the relevant technical guidelines. Electrically powered knapsack sprayers are now commercially available, but none have been formally evaluated for indoor residual spraying (IRS) inside buildings. Interim specifications are provided for organizations interested in testing these units to eliminate the need for manual pumping associated with compression sprayers. Electric sprayers can be used for residual wall spraying and larvicide application. An additional lance may be attached to extend the length for specific applications. Electrically powered knapsack sprayers must meet certain requirements. The filter should prevent nozzle blockages (a 50-mesh filter is typically sufficient) and be positioned deep enough to allow the operator to see the liquid level when the tank is filled to its maximum capacity. The filter diameter should match the filler opening of the spray tank. Instructions for recharging should be included in the user manual. A battery management system should be in place to prevent overcharging and overheating, ensuring the battery remains in good condition and has a long lifespan. Ideally, the battery should fully recharge within four hours, although overnight recharging is common. A battery power indicator on the sprayer would be beneficial. The materials used to construct the pump must be tested to confirm compatibility with pesticide formulations used in vector control. The spray tank typically has a capacity of 15 liters, and the filler hole should be at least 90 mm wide. The sprayer should be capable of delivering 5 liters of water to cover a 250 m² surface area during IRS. Lithium-ion batteries are lightweight and provide adequate power but are subject to restrictions, such as being unsuitable for air transport. Alternatives like lead-acid gel batteries are heavier and may be less efficient for recharging. Areas using this equipment should have a reliable electricity supply for battery recharging, and a set of replacement batteries may be necessary. A secondary filter should be installed near the nozzle to prevent blockages during spraying, and all filters should be easily accessible for frequent cleaning. An extension lance should be available to facilitate ceiling spraying, and a lance with a downward-angled attachment can be supplied for larviciding. The nozzle tip and flow rate must comply with international standards and be clearly declared.
